2610.30243.title: The coupled impacts of atmospheric dynamics and cloud microphysics on hot Jupiter atmospheres. I. An application to WASP-43b

These T-P profiles are used as the atmospheric structure input for our 1D CARMA simulations.

Each line color corresponds to a different condensing species labeled correspondingly. pFe and pCr refer to “pure Fe” and “pure Cr”, and are the homogeneously nucleating versions of Fe and Cr which otherwise nucleate heterogeneously. Clouds condense at all four modeled longitudes of WASP-43b, although the anti-stellar point generally hosts a higher number density of clouds and a wider variety of species.

Figure 5: These two-dimensional projections show the particle size distributions for the condensing cloud species at different longitudinal points on WASP-43b predicted by our 1D CARMA simulations. Each differently colored distribution is labeled according to its corresponding species. The different layers in each species’ distribution, as seen from the colorbar, shows the number density per bin of differently sized particles (x-axis) at varying pressures (y-axis). The intensity of colors shown in the colorbar is the same for all species. Most of the species that condense in the atmosphere of WASP-43b show varying particle size distributions that differ from a typically assumed lognormal distribution.

Figure 6: These plots show the pressure-averaged particle size distributions of the cloud species modeled by CARMA at different locations in the atmosphere. These distributions are plotted as normalized number densities as a function of particle radius. Each species’ size distribution generally shows non-lognormal behavior, with some species like Al2O3 and Mg2SiO4 displaying double peaks, making it challenging to parameterize these distributions with a single functional formula.

Figure 7: The distribution of cloud optical depth per layer shown across longitudes and pressures, averaged over all latitudes and over the wavelength band for JWST/MIRI. The top plot shows this distribution for our global clouds case, where all four points from CARMA are used at longitudes 0$\degree$, 90$\degree$, 180$\degree$, 270$\degree$ and longitudinally interpolated. The bottom plot shows the distribution for our nightside clouds case, where we only interpolate the nightside CARMA clouds centered at longitude 180$\degree$. As a result, fewer clouds are visible at non-nightside phases in our post-processing. The cloud optical depth appears very similar between the JWST/MIRI and HST/WFC3 bandpasses.

Figure 8: Synthetic emission spectra of the dayside/secondary-eclipse of WASP-43b made with PICASO in the HST/WFC3 wavelength band. The observed HST/WFC3 emission spectrum from Kreidberg et al. [79] and Stevenson et al. [141] is overplotted as black dots. Note that here, the cloud-free spectrum and nightside clouds spectrum overlap completely because the nightside clouds are not visible from the dayside phase. The spectra with cloud-free daysides (cloud-free and nightside clouds) match the dayside observations much better than the spectrum with a cloudy dayside (global clouds), although a cloud-free dayside over-predicts the flux at some wavelengths.

Figure 9: Synthetic emission spectra from our three different post-processed models of WASP-43b from PICASO, shown at different phases of the orbit in the HST/WFC3 wavelength band. The black dots are the HST/WFC3 data from Stevenson et al. [141], and each model (cloud-free, global clouds, nightside clouds) is plotted with a different linestyle. The nightside phases (45$\degree$, 315$\degree$) show the poorest match between our modeled spectra and the data, though generally favoring a cloudy nightside. The data for the dayside phases (135$\degree$, 225$\degree$) seems to be best explained by a cloud-free dayside. Our nightside clouds model, where we only include CARMA clouds on the nightside during post-processing, provide the best explanation for observations out of all our models.

Figure 10: Synthetic emission spectra of WASP-43b made with PICASO at different phases in the JWST/MIRI band. The observed JWST/MIRI emission spectra from Bell et al. [17] are overplotted as black dots. A comparison to the data seems to indicate little to no clouds on the dayside, as well as a cloudy nightside featuring a silicate absorption feature at 9-10.5 $\mu$m (in alignment with the HST/WFC3 observations, seen in Figures 8 and 9). The morning and evening limbs are generally best explained by our nightside clouds case, where we post-process the atmosphere with only clouds predicted by CARMA on the nightside.

2610.30243.abstract: Understanding the influence of cloud-circulation feedback on planetary climates is crucial to interpreting solar system and extrasolar planet observations. Hot Jupiter phase curve observations have reported westward optical phase curve offsets and weak absorption features, which may be explained by the presence of clouds. JWST observations have also revealed tentative silicate cloud absorption features in emission and transmission spectroscopy. While a number of 3D atmospheric dynamics models of hot Jupiters and microphysical models describing cloud formation exist, few combine these two approaches. To help elucidate the impact of clouds on hot Jupiters, we introduce a post-processing scheme with the 3D GCM ADAM with SPARC (formerly SPARC/MITgcm), the 1D microphysical cloud model CARMA, and the radiative transfer code PICASO. We first simulate the cloud-free atmosphere of WASP-43b with ADAM, then incorporate resulting thermal profiles into CARMA to simulate WASP-43b's cloud structure, and finally generate phase-dependent emission spectra from our results with PICASO. By comparing to JWST observations, we infer that WASP-43b has a cloudy nightside, a mostly clear morning and evening limb with patchy clouds, and a clear dayside at the level of the photosphere. Our microphysical model predicts the condensation of five cloud species, including silicates, but overestimates the cloud opacity at all phases compared to observations, requiring additional modeling to explain. The results from this post-processing setup are promising for more meaningful characterization of WASP-43b's atmosphere, and will serve as a comparison baseline for our upcoming indirect coupling of both models, as well as for other future studies.

2610.30310.abstract: We present Keck/NIRC2 adaptive optics imaging results of planetary microlensing event OGLE-2012-BLG-0563. We find that the OGLE-2012-BLG-0563L planetary system consists of a 1.12 +/- 0.09 Jupiter-mass planet orbiting a 0.81 +/- 0.04 solar-mass host star at a distance of 5.49 +/- 0.56 kpc from the Sun. This event has a lens-source separation of 23.28 +/- 0.48 mas, which is the smallest lens-source separation measured to date with Keck AO data. We find that the incorrect solution - which identifies the Northeast (NE) star as the source star - is favored if one only considers the discovery paper, the Fukui et al. (2015) solution, or an unconstrained model. However, by performing an image-constrained light curve model fit using the relative proper motion direction constraint from the Keck follow-up data, we demonstrate that the correct solution identifies the NE star as the lens star. The discrepancy in the unconstrained models is driven by systematics in the FTS and MOA B & C data, alongside the impact of the relative proper motion direction constraints. This outcome offers two important lessons for future Roman data analysis: (1) thoroughly verify systematics across all passbands and identify the precise origin of chi-squared differences, and (2) utilize image-constrained light curve modeling incorporating relative proper motion direction constraints to identify the correct lens.

2610.30494.abstract: The three-dimensional shapes of Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs) are notoriously difficult to determine due to their slow orbital motion and minimal variations in aspect angle over human timescales. To overcome this geometric degeneracy, we developed a versatile modeling framework capable of deriving ellipsoidal shapes by simultaneously combining stellar occultations and rotational light curves, including parameterizations of localized surface albedo. We applied this methodology to the large TNO (50000) Quaoar, jointly modeling 37 stellar occultation events and two photometric datasets. Our MCMC analysis demonstrates that Quaoar is best represented by a triaxial shape with equatorial semi-axes $a = 620.7^{+3.3}_{-2.8}$ km and $b = 546.5^{+6.0}_{-5.6}$ km, and a polar semi-axis $c = 511.5^{+5.3}_{-5.5}$ km, yielding a bulk density of $1.663 \pm 0.127$ g cm$^{-3}$. By isolating Quaoar's barycentric motion from the astrometric offsets, we determined the mass of its satellite, Weywot, to be $(1.485 \pm 0.360) \times 10^{18}$ kg, corresponding to a system mass ratio of $q = 0.0012 \pm 0.0003$ and a satellite bulk density of $0.95 \pm 0.60$ g cm$^{-3}$. Furthermore, dynamical simulations using the derived triaxial gravitational field reveal that potential additional satellites can only maintain stable orbits beyond 2.4 Quaoar radii, as inner bodies would be strongly perturbed. Regarding the ring system, particles at the location of the secondary ring (Q2R) location exhibit libration associated with the 5:7 spin-orbit resonance (SOR). Similarly, particles at the location of the main ring (Q1R) location show libration of the 2:6 SOR angle for orbital eccentricities larger than 0.2, providing a plausible mechanism for the azimuthal width variations observed in Q1R.

2610.30515.abstract: We examine the long-term evolution of localized eccentricity perturbations in a softened Laplace-Lagrange chain. The secular coupling between mass elements is long-ranged, suggesting that any disturbance imposed at a single radius should disperse rapidly across the chain. We show that this expectation fails once the secular interaction is regularized by a finite softening length $\beta$: while broad eccentricity profiles propagate smoothly, as textbook secular theory anticipates, narrow profiles remain confined to their launching site for millions of secular periods. The origin of this quasi-localization lies in the dispersion relation of the softened chain. The group velocity of eccentricity waves collapses by orders of magnitude on spatial scales below the softening length, so that narrow perturbations project almost entirely onto a nearly flat sector of the band, where little differential precession is available to disperse them. Propagating the initial wavenumber spectrum through the dispersion relation reproduces the retained fraction of angular momentum deficit across the full range of perturbation widths with no adjustable parameters. The confined perturbation is flanked by an apsidally polarized (oppositely-aligned) response, which we show to be the real-space imprint of this spectral projection. The softening length therefore sets a dynamical scale below which eccentricity perturbations spread only on timescales far longer than the secular period.

2610.30871.abstract: The European Space Agency Comet Interceptor mission is designed to fly-by an as-yet undetermined incoming long-period or dynamically-new comet, which will require an accurate prediction of its trajectory. Cometary orbits are perturbed from purely gravitational trajectories by non-gravitational accelerations (NGAs) stemming from their outgassing, however, and these must be taken into account in the navigation. We here test the ability of ground-based astrometry and standard NGA-fitting techniques to predict the position and velocity of incoming comets perturbed by a Monte Carlo sampled thermophysical acceleration model. We find that, due to the difficulties of predicting NGA evolution as well as the limitations of reasonably simulated astrometry, predicted accuracies are unlikely to meet the mission goals of 1000 km and 1 m s$^{-1}$ in position and velocity, sixty days before intercept. We instead recommend expanded uncertainties of $10,000$ km and several m s$^{-1}$. Our NGA fits struggle to reproduce the reference accelerations and trajectories when outgassing is rising steeply at a few AU-incoming, but with more observations up until perihelion, do eventually converge, leading to good estimates of many of the underlying acceleration parameters even for half an orbital arc.

2610.30936.abstract: How do infrasound signals from fireballs relate to atmospheric entry conditions and the physical properties of their parents meteoroids? In this study, we investigate the detectability of infrasound generated by local-to-regional fireballs and use the associated signals to constrain meteoroid physical properties. Across Western Australia and California, the Global Fireball Observatory (GFO) recorded nearly 300 fireball events with well-constrained trajectories within 500 km of an infrasound array over an 11-year period. Of these, 20 fireballs were confidently associated with infrasound detections. For these events, we estimate energies, constrain source altitudes using atmospheric ray-tracing simulations, and investigate source mechanisms using a multi-diagnostic approach. In particular, we examine whether the recorded infrasonic signals originated from cylindrical line sources (ballistic shocks) or discrete fragmentation episodes. Our results show that infrasound-detected fireballs span a broad range of dynamical and physical properties. This variability indicates that infrasound detectability is governed by a combination of source characteristics, atmospheric propagation conditions, and source-receiver geometry, rather than any single entry parameter. Analysis of the fireball shock source mechanisms reveals an even contribution from both ballistic and fragmentation-related sources. These results also demonstrate the value of combining infrasound and optical observations for robust constraints on meteoroid shock generation processes.

2610.31006.abstract: In this work, we survey M-type stars within 15 pc observed by Gaia based on their colour, magnitude, and quality of astrometric data. We aim to detect new substellar companions using primarily Gaia astrometry and, when available, proper-motion anomaly (PMa) along with radial velocity (RV) and direct imaging (DI) data. We used the GaiaPMEX tool to search for bound companions around 582 M dwarfs. We identified all previously known stellar and planetary companions that were consistent with the Gaia excess signal. Then for all newly identified companions, we computed detection limits in the (mass, semi-major axis) parameter space using archival RV and DI data, to possibly rule out the presence of a stellar companion. The joint analysis of the parameter space allowed by astrometry and constrained by RV and DI provides tight constraints on the nature of the companion. We found 156 M dwarfs to have a bound companion within the Gaia sensitivity domain. The astrometric signals of 37 and seven of them are due to known stellar and substellar companions, respectively. We report 35 new substellar companions among which at least ten giant planets orbiting between 0.2 au and 2 au, with masses close to 1 M_Jup. We also report 77 substellar candidates, and provide detection limits using astrometry+RV+DI for 50 stars with known exoplanets and no significant Gaia excess noise. This work reveals a significant population of new substellar companions to M-type stars, challenging core accretion models. These results will be crucial inputs for estimating occurrence rates and studying the architecture of planetary systems around M dwarfs. Some new companions presented here, located beyond the water ice line, are prime targets for DI or coronagraphy observations with JWST or ELT.

2610.31286.abstract: Direct detection and characterization of exoplanet atmospheres via reflected starlight enables probes of composition of mature exoplanet systems (since flux is decoupled from age) at closer separations than via thermal emission (due to observations in visible wavelengths), and even probes of biosignatures. New and upcoming ground and space-based platforms are enabling these observations for the first time. Recently the 3-m Lazuli Space Telescope, from the Eric and Wendy Schmidt Observatory System, was announced, which will be equipped with the ExtraSolar Coronagraph (ESC) designed for reflected light gas giant exoplanet observations in visible wavelengths. In this paper we present 27 known giant exoplanets that make up the first target list for these observations. Our target list spans ages and temperatures of planets not probed before by direct imaging, but some of which will also be accessible to the \textsl{Nancy Grace Roman} Coronagraph instrument and the ELT-METIS thermal imager, providing comprehensive atmosphere characterization and synergies. We discuss the science enabled by ESC observations of our target list and enhancements provided by future astrometric and radial velocity measurements.

2610.31492.abstract: Constraining atmospheric loss is crucial for understanding the evolution of planetary atmospheres. We report the detection of an evaporating exosphere from TOI-3884b, a super-Neptune in a polar orbit around an M4 dwarf star. We infer this evaporation from a 6.8$\pm$0.27\% excess transit depth in the He I 10830 Å\, line, observed during five transits of TOI-3884b with the Habitable Zone Planet Finder spectrometer. While we observe outflow signatures starting as early as 5 hours before the onset of the planet's optical transit, no significant post-transit tail is detected. Hitherto, such a pre-transit headwind without a significant post-transit tail has only been detected from HAT-P-67b, a hot Saturn orbiting an F-type star. This asymmetric outflow morphology supports irradiation-driven mass loss over core-heated mass loss, and we explore whether this could be caused by sub-Alfvén star-planet interaction. The detection of such complex outflow morphologies is now opening a new window, enabling us to test theories of star-planet interactions and planetary magnetic fields with observations.

2610.30372.abstract: The Pandora SmallSat is a NASA flight project designed to study the atmospheres of exoplanets. Transmission spectroscopy of transiting exoplanets provides our best opportunity to identify the makeup of planetary atmospheres in the coming decade, and is a key science driver for HST and JWST. Stellar photospheric inhomogeneity due to star spots, however, has been shown to contaminate the observed spectra in these high-precision measurements. Pandora will address the problem of stellar contamination by collecting long-duration photometric observations sampled over a stellar rotation period with a visible-light channel and simultaneous spectra with a near-IR channel. These simultaneous multiwavelength observations will constrain star spot covering fractions of exoplanet host stars, enabling star and planet signals to be disentangled in transmission spectra to then reliably determine exoplanet atmosphere compositions. Pandora will observe exoplanets with sizes ranging from Earth-size to Jupiter-size and host stars spanning mid-K to late-M spectral types. Pandora was selected in early 2021 as part of NASA's inaugural Astrophysics Pioneers Program. Herein, we present an overview of the mission, including the science objectives, operations, the observatory, science planning, and upcoming milestones as we prepare for launch readiness in 2025.

2610.30506.abstract: Magnetic interaction between astrophysical objects can play an important role and produce electromagnetic radiation in various systems, ranging from planet-moon and star-planet systems to binary compact objects. We extend our previous numerical study of an ideal magnetized plasma flowing past a conducting sphere to the case where the sphere is magnetized. Such a flow generates magnetic disturbances and produces a drag force on the sphere. We examine the drag coefficient as a function of the strength and orientation of the conductor's internal magnetic field relative to the background magnetic field. We find that a strong internal magnetic field that is aligned with the background field significantly enhances the drag coefficient compared to the unmagnetized case; this enhancement is related to the increased magnetic flux that connects the conductor and the open, external field region. We also explore how the drag coefficient changes as the flow transitions from the sub-Alfvénic to the super-Alfvénic regime. Our results suggest that magnetic interaction may play a larger role in orbital evolution of some binary systems than previously expected.

2610.30594.abstract: Stellar oscillations and granulation are key probes of stellar convection, one of the most poorly understood processes in stars. Stellar models predict strong wavelength dependence of the amplitudes of oscillations and granulation, but hitherto both processes have only been measured at optical wavelengths. Here we present the first detection of oscillations and granulation at infrared wavelengths, using JWST time-series observations of the F6V main-sequence star WASP-121 that were obtained to study the atmosphere of an exoplanet. We find that the amplitudes of oscillations and granulation decrease with wavelength, consistent with expectations, but with a functional form that deviates from simple blackbody scaling. The detection opens the door to detailed tests of 3D convection models, facilitates the combined modeling of stellar and exoplanet signals in JWST passbands for exoplanet observations, and supports the predicted asteroseismic yields from the infrared time-domain data that will soon be obtained by the Roman Space Telescope.

2610.30806.title: Astrometric detection of rocky exoplanets from inexpensive space platforms

figures.caption:
Figure 1: Schematic diagram of the Fragmented Pupil telescope concept. Left Panel: Bright stars available over $\sim$degree scale optical fields are condensed into an artificial cluster at sub-arcminute scales (red box). Middle Panel: This is accomplished in a single reflection from a high-stability tessellated optical surface aboard a stable space telescope. Right Panel: Precision astrometric monitoring can then be accomplished by analysis of the resulting well-sampled interferograms in the image plane.
Here the central science target is surrounded by a set of 6 reference stars, condensed to lie at arcsecond scales.

2610.30806.abstract: The detection of orbiting exoplanets by way of astrometric monitoring of the host star to reveal gravitationally induced reflex motion requires extreme precision and measurement stability when targeting Earth-mass objects. Despite this, astrometry is widely regarded as the most promising avenue for the most desired of all targets: true Earth analogue systems in the solar neighbourhood. Formerly thought to require flagship class investment, recently several smaller concepts such as the TOLIMAN and SHERA missions have shown that detections are possible, at least in principle, from more modest space platforms. A key enabling feature is that these missions exploit narrow-angle astrometry. Observing only multiple star systems where the target provides its own astrometric reference greatly alleviates the challenges confronted by traditional astrometry with its reliance on distant, faint field stars. This principle underlies the TOLIMAN mission, for which progress and status is reported. However, only a tiny handful of nearby star systems are suited to such a TOLIMAN-like architecture. This paper discusses speculative optical concepts featuring ultra-stable telescopes of modest (<0.5m) aperture designed for astrometric monitoring of isolated single stars at the micro-arcsecond scales required for the discovery of Earth mass objects orbiting sun-like stars in temperate orbits. In simulation, highly sought-after neighbourhood systems such as Epsilon Eridani and Tau Ceti can be exhaustively searched for rocky planets with dedicated observing campaigns spanning several years, all from relatively inexpensive orbital platforms.
